subtype: Approach: writing the schedule on a shared chart [Action]
passage:
Sunday. Sarita took a sheet of paper and a ruler and drew a table: seven days across, two names down the side, blue for Madhav and orange for herself. Under each day she coloured the boxes for the tablet: half an hour each. She stuck it on the fridge with a magnet.

Tuesday. Madhav opened the fridge, looked at the boxes and said, "It's blue today, right?" "Yes," said Sarita. No argument.

Next Sunday. They coloured the new week together. "Better than shouting," said Madhav. Sarita nodded.

qa.q: Which colour stands for Madhav on the chart?
How did Sarita probably feel when Madhav checked the chart without arguing?
qa.a: Sarita was probably pleased and relieved, since the chart settled the question with 'Yes' and no argument.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the children use if the chart is forgotten, and why?
qa.a: They could ask a parent to check the chart or use a kitchen timer for each turn. A neutral helper stops small disagreements from growing.

qa.q: How does the chart feel to Madhav?
qa.a: Madhav checked it calmly and said it was better than shouting, so Madhav finds it fair and easy to follow.

grounding: A girl draws a weekly table with names and colours on the fridge, so the children can check the written plan instead of arguing from memory.

subtype: Approach: writing the schedule on a shared chart [Action]
passage: Preeti, you're asking why my fridge still has that yellowed paper chart on the side. Sit, and your Vinita Nani will tell you. When I was a girl, we got our first fridge, and with it, my brother and I got our first fights about turns. Not about the fridge; about the radio on top of it. Every evening he said it was his turn, and I said it was mine, and nobody could remember. So one Sunday I took a ruler and made a table. Seven days across. His name in blue, mine in red. I stuck it to the fridge with flour paste. After that, when he said "my turn," I just pointed. The chart settled it. Nobody argued with a chart.

qa.q: What colour was Vinita's name on the chart?
How did young Vinita probably feel before she made the chart?
qa.a: She probably felt frustrated and tired of arguing, since nobody could remember whose turn it was.

qa.q: What turning point settled the arguments in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Making the written chart was the turning point, because both children could check it instead of relying on memory.

qa.q: How might Vinita's brother have seen the chart?
qa.a: Her brother may have been annoyed at first, then accepted it, since it showed his turns clearly too.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a girl, she drew a coloured weekly chart of turns and stuck it on the fridge so the siblings could check instead of argue.

subtype: Approach: writing the schedule on a shared chart [Action]
passage: The family laptop in Rehana's flat was shared by three children, and nobody could remember who had it last. Then the power cuts started, two hours every evening, and the fights got worse. On Saturday Rehana took chart paper and drew a table: days down the side, time slots across, only the hours when there was power. She gave each person a colour. Samir, who was five and couldn't read yet, got green, so he could find his own squares. She stuck it on the fridge with magnets. That evening, when the power came back, Samir ran to the fridge, put his finger on a green square, and said, "Mine." Nobody argued.

qa.q: What colour did Samir get on the chart?
Why did Rehana give each person a colour?
qa.a: She wanted everyone, even little Samir who couldn't read, to check the chart; she seems thoughtful and hopeful it would end the fights.

qa.q: What else could Rehana do if the power cut times change?
qa.a: She could leave a few blank slots to fill in each week, so the chart can change without starting over.

qa.q: How does the chart look to Samir?
qa.a: Samir feels proud and included, able to find his own green squares without asking anyone.

grounding: It shows a girl drawing a coloured weekly table on the fridge so the children can check turns instead of arguing from memory.
